title: Calm About AI: How Ready Are You?
subtitle: A 3-minute check of your everyday AI habits. Based on the textbook Artificial Intelligence in Public Health by Min Wu (Springer, 2026).
note: An informal self-check, not a formal assessment.

levels.label: Just Starting
levels.feedback: AI can feel overwhelming, and that's normal. Start with one habit: when an AI answer matters, check it with another source.
levels.next_read: Chapter 1 (what AI is) and Chapter 9 (trusting AI)

levels.label: Curious
levels.feedback: You know the basics. Next habit: before trusting an AI tool, ask where its data came from and who might be missing.

levels.label: Careful User
levels.feedback: You use AI with good judgment. Keep tasting the dish: ask why, check, then decide yourself.

levels.label: Calm Navigator
levels.feedback: You're ready for the AI era. You know when to trust AI, when to say no, and that you stay responsible. Share these habits with others.
levels.next_read: The full book, or help a colleague take this check

items.stem: A chatbot cites a study that doesn't exist. This is called a...
items.explanation: AI can make things up and present them as real.

items.stem: AI hallucinations usually sound...
items.explanation: That's why they're easy to miss. Check before you trust.

items.stem: Giving a chatbot your own trusted documents to answer from is called...
items.explanation: RAG points the AI to sources you choose.

items.stem: True or false: Even with RAG, you should still check the answer.
items.explanation: True. RAG reduces mistakes but doesn't remove them.

items.stem: "IF blood pressure > 140/90, THEN flag hypertension." Who wrote this rule?
items.explanation: Rule-based systems follow rules written by experts.

items.stem: In machine learning, who writes the rules?
options: No one; there are no rules
items.explanation: People wrote rules; machine learning learns them from data.

items.stem: Rule-based systems are easy to...
items.explanation: You can read the rule. But someone must rewrite it by hand.

items.stem: A no-show model learns from past appointments marked...
items.explanation: AI learns from examples where the answer is already known.

items.stem: Testing a model on new patients checks whether it...
options: Works beyond what it learned from
items.explanation: Doing well on old data doesn't guarantee doing well on new data.

items.stem: A neural network learns by adjusting its...
items.explanation: The weights are its recipe, tuned during training.

items.stem: An AI trained only at big-city hospitals may struggle at...
items.explanation: AI suits situations it has seen, not new ones.

items.stem: "Black box" means...
options: It's hard to see how AI decides
The AI is kept secret by law
items.explanation: This is why many doctors hesitate to trust AI.

items.stem: The "deep" in deep learning means...
items.explanation: More layers let the network learn richer patterns.

items.stem: Transformers, the engine behind chatbots, read each word in...
options: Isolation, one word at a time
items.explanation: Self-attention lets each word look at the words around it.

items.stem: ChatGPT is...
options: An app built on GPT models
items.explanation: Transformer = design, GPT = model family, ChatGPT = app.

items.stem: True or false: A chatbot's fluent answer proves it understands like a human.
items.explanation: False. It's still a neural network trained on data.

items.stem: Public health problems are messy, so AI often combines...
items.explanation: Rules keep policy and fairness; data finds new patterns.

items.stem: AI is only as good as its...
items.explanation: Data writes the recipe.

items.stem: Garbage in, ...
items.explanation: AI learns from whatever it gets, good or bad.

items.stem: A nurse types blood pressure 410/80 instead of 140/80. The AI will likely...
options: Give a wrong answer for this patient
items.explanation: Bad data can enter twice: in training and in today's entry.

items.stem: Which is "story" (unstructured) data?
items.explanation: Notes, images and recordings are stories; codes and times are forms.

items.stem: During a flu outbreak, data that arrives weeks late is...
items.explanation: In fast events, timing matters as much as accuracy.

items.stem: "John Smith" and "Jon Smith" have the same birthday. You should...
options: Check and merge if it's one person
items.explanation: Duplicates split a patient's history. Clean data starts at the front desk.

items.stem: To predict hospital readmissions, which data helps most?
items.explanation: Useful data must fit the question.

items.stem: A vendor's AI worked well at other hospitals. What should you do first?
options: Test it on your own patients
items.explanation: A popular sepsis alert worked worse at one hospital than promised.

items.stem: A skin-condition AI learned mostly from light skin. It may...
options: Make more mistakes on darker skin
items.explanation: AI works for people in the data and fails the rest.

items.stem: Using past spending to find the sickest patients can miss people who...
items.explanation: Cost is not need. Measure what you mean.

items.stem: Before trusting AI, ask: who is ___ from the data?
items.explanation: Uninsured and rural patients are often left out.

items.stem: True or false: Addiction treatment records have extra privacy protection beyond HIPAA.
items.explanation: True. A federal rule (42 CFR Part 2) adds protection.

items.stem: Before buying an AI tool, which question protects patients most?
options: Does it have a mobile app?
Does patient data leave our system?
items.explanation: Ask who sees the data, where it goes, and whether patients agreed.

items.stem: People usually adopt a new tool if it's...
items.explanation: These two questions guided adoption of older tools.

items.stem: Old tools stay the same. AI can...
options: Change as it learns from new data
items.explanation: Old tools: you adapt to them. AI adapts to you.

items.stem: We can print every number inside an AI, but we can't...
items.explanation: The black box isn't hidden. It's unreadable.

items.stem: An AI-supported decision goes wrong. Who is responsible?
items.explanation: AI is a tool. You stay responsible.

items.stem: Accepting every AI answer without checking is...
items.explanation: Trust should match how reliable the AI really is.

items.stem: Good trust in AI means...
options: Trust it when it's reliable; say no when it's not
items.explanation: Not more trust. The right amount.

items.stem: When evidence is thin, a good AI should...
items.explanation: A good partner names what's missing and leaves the call to you.

items.stem: Which question needs the most care with a chatbot?
items.explanation: High stakes plus a confident wrong answer can cause real harm.

items.stem: Which is a healthy AI habit?
options: Ask until it agrees with you
Ask why, check another source, decide yourself
items.explanation: The AI makes the dish. You taste it before serving.

items.stem: True or false: If AI feels like a partner, it shares responsibility for decisions.
items.explanation: False. It feels like a partner, but it's a tool.
